title: “Like Summer Tempests Came His Tears”
paragraphs: The Rat reached out one neat little brown paw, took a firm hold of Toad by the scruff of his neck, and heaved with all his might. Slowly but surely the dripping Toad came up over the edge of the hole, until at last he was standing safe and sound in the front hall. He was streaked with mud and pond weed, of course, and water poured off him in streams. But he was as happy and high-spirited as ever, now that he was in a friend’s house again, with no more dodging and ducking. He was free to throw off a disguise that was beneath his dignity and took so much effort to keep up.

“Oh, Ratty!” he cried. “You can’t imagine the times I’ve had since I last saw you! Such trials, such sufferings, and all of them so nobly borne! And then such escapes, such disguises, such tricks, and all so cleverly planned and carried out! Thrown in prison—and escaped, naturally! Thrown into a canal—and swam to shore! Stole a horse—and sold him for a huge sum of money! Fooled everybody—made them all do exactly what I wanted! Oh, I _am_ a clever Toad, and no mistake! Guess what my latest exploit was! Just wait till I tell you——”

“Toad,” said the Water Rat, seriously and firmly, “you go upstairs right now, take off that old cotton rag that looks as though it once belonged to some washerwoman. Scrub yourself thoroughly, put on some of my clothes, and try to come down looking like a gentleman, if you _can._ Because in my whole life I have never laid eyes on a shabbier, muddier, more disreputable-looking creature than you! Now stop showing off and arguing, and go! I’ll have something to say to you later!”

At first Toad was inclined to stay and talk back. He’d had quite enough of being ordered around in prison, and here it was starting all over again, it seemed, and from a Rat, too! But then he caught sight of himself in the mirror over the hat-stand, with the shabby black bonnet perched at a jaunty angle over one eye, and he changed his mind and went very quickly and meekly up to the Rat’s dressing-room. There he gave himself a thorough wash and brush-up and changed his clothes, and then stood for a long while in front of the mirror, admiring himself with pride and pleasure and thinking what complete fools everyone must have been to mistake him, even for a moment, for a washerwoman.

By the time he came downstairs again, lunch was on the table, and Toad was very glad to see it, for he had been through some difficult times and had done a great deal of hard exercise since the excellent breakfast the gypsy had given him. While they ate, Toad told the Rat all his adventures, dwelling mostly on his own cleverness, his presence of mind in emergencies, and his cunning in tight spots, and rather making it sound as though he’d had a merry and thrilling time of it. But the more he talked and boasted, the more serious and silent the Rat became.

When at last Toad had talked himself to a standstill, there was a silence for a while. Then the Rat said, “Now, Toady, I don’t want to hurt you, after everything you’ve already been through; but seriously, don’t you see what a perfect fool you’ve been making of yourself? By your own account you’ve been handcuffed, locked up, starved, chased, frightened out of your wits, insulted, laughed at, and thrown into the water in a most undignified way—by a woman, too! Where’s the amusement in that? Where’s the fun? And all because you just had to go and steal a motor-car. You know very well you’ve never had anything but trouble from motor-cars since the moment you first set eyes on one. But if you _will_ get mixed up with them—and you usually do, within five minutes of starting out—why _steal_ them? Be a cripple, if you find that exciting; go bankrupt, for a change, if you’ve set your heart on it; but why choose to be a convict? When are you going to be sensible, think of your friends, and try to be a credit to them? Do you imagine it’s any pleasure for me, for instance, to hear other animals saying, wherever I go, that I’m the fellow who keeps company with jailbirds?”

Now, here was one very reassuring thing about Toad: he was a truly kind-hearted creature, and he never held it against his real friends when they gave him a talking-to. Even when his heart was most firmly set on something, he could always see the matter from the other side. So even though, the whole time Rat was holding forth so earnestly, Toad kept muttering stubbornly to himself, “But it _was_ fun, all the same! Terrific fun!” and letting out peculiar, smothered noises from somewhere inside, k-i-ck-ck-ck, and poop-p-p, sounds a bit like choked snorts or soda-water bottles being uncorked, he nevertheless sighed deeply as soon as Rat was completely finished, and said, in a most polite and humble voice, “You’re quite right, Ratty! You are always so _wise_! Yes, I’ve been a vain old ass, I see that plainly; but from now on I mean to be a good Toad and give it all up. As for motor-cars, I haven’t cared half so much for them since I got dunked in that river of yours the other time. The truth is, as I clung to the rim of your hole, trying to catch my breath, a sudden thought struck me—a really dazzling thought—having to do with motor-boats—now, now! Don’t carry on so, old fellow, and stomp, and knock things over; it was only a thought, and we won’t say another word about it today. We’ll have our coffee, _and_ a smoke, and a peaceful chat, and then I’ll amble down to Toad Hall, change into my own clothes, and get everything running again as it always did. I’ve had my fill of adventures. From now on my life will be calm, steady, and respectable: I’ll putter around my estate, improve it, and do a little landscape gardening from time to time. There will always be some dinner waiting for my friends whenever they visit; and I’ll keep a pony-cart for jogging around the countryside, exactly as I did in the good old days, before I turned restless and started wanting to _do_ things.”
“Stroll quietly down to Toad Hall?” cried the Rat, in great excitement. “Whatever are you talking about? Are you telling me you really haven’t _heard?_”
“Heard what?” said Toad, going rather pale. “Out with it, Ratty! Quickly! Don’t hold anything back! What is it I haven’t heard?”
“Do you really mean,” shouted the Rat, thumping the table with his little fist, “that you’ve heard nothing at all about the Stoats and Weasels?”
What, the Wild Wooders?” cried Toad, shaking from head to foot. “No, not one word! What have they been doing?”
“—And how they’ve gone and taken over Toad Hall?” the Rat went on.
Toad propped his elbows on the table and rested his chin on his paws; a big tear gathered in each eye, spilled over, and dropped onto the table, plop! plop!
“Go on, Ratty,” he murmured after a moment. “Tell me everything. The worst is over. I’m an animal again. I can bear it.”

“When you—got—yourself into that—that—difficulty,” said the Rat, in a slow, weighty voice, “what I mean is, when you—vanished from society for a while, because of that misunderstanding over a—a machine, you know—”
Toad only nodded.

“Well, naturally it was talked about a good deal down here,” the Rat went on, “not only along the riverside but even in the Wild Wood. The animals took sides, as always happens. The River-bankers stood up for you and said you’d been shamefully treated and that there was no justice to be had in the country these days. But the Wild Wood animals said nasty things, and that it served you right, and that it was high time this sort of thing was stopped. And they got very cocky, and went around saying you were finished this time! You’d never come back, never, never!”
Toad nodded once more and said nothing.

“That’s the kind of nasty little animals they are,” the Rat said. “But Mole and Badger refused to give up, through every sort of trouble; they swore that you would be back before long, one way or another. How, they couldn’t say, but somehow!”
Toad began to sit up in his chair again and to smirk a little.

“They reasoned from history,” the Rat said. “Never once, they pointed out, had a criminal law managed to beat brazen cheek and glib talk like yours, backed by a heavy purse. So they made plans to bring their belongings over to Toad Hall, sleep there, air the place out, and have everything ready for the moment you showed up. Naturally they never imagined what would happen, though they did distrust the Wild Wood animals. And now I’ve reached the saddest and most tragic part of my tale. On one dark night—a _very_ dark night, with a howling wind and rain simply pouring down—a gang of weasels, armed to the teeth, tiptoed up the carriage-drive to the front entrance. At that same moment, a troop of desperate ferrets came across the kitchen-garden and took control of the backyard and the servants’ quarters; and a company of skirmishing stoats, who would stop at nothing, took over the conservatory and the billiard-room and guarded the French windows leading out to the lawn.

“The Mole and the Badger were sitting by the fire in the smoking-room, swapping stories and suspecting nothing, since it was no night for any creature to be outdoors, when those bloodthirsty villains smashed down the doors and burst in on them from all sides. They fought as well as they could, but what good was it? They had no weapons, they were caught off guard, and what can two animals do against hundreds? The villains grabbed them and beat them hard with sticks, those two poor faithful creatures, and threw them out into the cold and the wet, hurling insults and rude remarks after them!”
At this point the hard-hearted Toad let out a snicker, then recovered himself and did his best to put on a very solemn face.

“Ever since then,” the Rat went on, “the Wild Wooders have been living in Toad Hall and doing exactly as they please! They stay in bed till the afternoon, they eat breakfast whenever the mood strikes them, and the house is in such a state (so I hear) that you wouldn’t want anyone to see it! They’re getting through your food and your drink, cracking cheap jokes at your expense, and bellowing rude songs about—well, about prisons and judges and policemen. Nasty, personal songs, and not a bit funny. And they’ve been informing the shopkeepers and anyone else who’ll listen that they’re here to stay.”
“Oh, are they, now!” cried Toad, jumping up and grabbing a stick. “I’ll put a stop to that in no time!”
“There’s no point, Toad!” the Rat called after him. “Come back here and sit down; all you’ll do is land yourself in trouble.”

But Toad was gone, and there was no holding him. He marched quickly down the road with his stick over his shoulder, fuming and muttering to himself in his anger, until he came near his front gate, when suddenly a long yellow ferret with a gun popped up from behind the fence.
“Who goes there?” said the ferret sharply.
“Rubbish!” said Toad, furious. “How dare you speak to me that way? Get out of there this instant, or else I’ll——”
The ferret didn’t say a single word. He simply lifted his gun to his shoulder. Toad had the good sense to throw himself flat on the road, and—_Bang!_—a bullet whizzed past just above him.

Toad leaped up, badly shaken, and bolted down the road as fast as his legs could carry him. Behind him he could hear the ferret chuckling, and then other nasty, thin little giggles picking up the sound and passing it along.
He went back, thoroughly crestfallen, and told the Water Rat.
“What did I tell you?” said the Rat. “It’s no use. They’ve posted sentries, and they’re all armed. You’ll just have to wait.”
All the same, Toad wasn’t ready to give up so quickly. He fetched the boat and rowed up the river toward the spot where the garden side of Toad Hall ran down to the water’s edge.

Once his old home came into view, he stopped rowing and let the boat drift while he carefully studied the shore. Everything looked calm, empty and still. The whole front of Toad Hall lay before him, shining in the evening sun. Pigeons were settling along the straight edge of the roof in little groups of two and three, the garden was bursting with flowers, and there was the creek running up to the boat-house, with the small wooden bridge across it. It was all peaceful and deserted, and it seemed to be simply waiting for him to come back. He decided to check the boat-house first. Very cautiously he paddled to the mouth of the creek, and he was just gliding beneath the bridge when—_Crash!_

A huge stone came plummeting down and smashed right through the bottom of the boat. The boat flooded and went under, and Toad was left thrashing about in deep water. He glanced up and spotted two stoats hanging over the bridge railing, gleefully watching him. “Next time it’ll be your head, Toady!” they shouted down. Furious, Toad swam for the bank. The stoats laughed and laughed, holding each other up, and then laughed some more, until they very nearly had two fits—that is, one fit each, of course.
Toad trudged back wearily on foot and told the Water Rat about his disappointing experiences once again.

“Well, _what_ did I tell you?” said the Rat, very crossly. “And now, just look at this! See what you’ve gone and done! You’ve lost me the boat I was so fond of, that’s what! And completely ruined that nice suit I lent you! Honestly, Toad, of all the maddening animals alive—it’s a wonder you have any friends left at all!”

At that moment Toad saw clearly how foolish and mistaken his behavior had been. He owned up to his errors and his pigheadedness, and he apologized fully to Rat for losing his boat and ruining his clothes. Then he finished off with the honest surrender that always melted his friend’s objections and won him back: “Ratty! I can see now that I’ve been a stubborn, willful Toad! From this moment on, believe me, I’ll be humble and obedient, and I won’t do a single thing without your kind advice and your full approval!”

“If you truly mean that,” said the kindhearted Rat, whose anger had already faded, “then here is my advice. Since it’s so late, sit down to your supper, which will be on the table in a minute, and be patient. I’m quite certain there’s nothing we can do until we’ve seen Mole and Badger, heard what they have to report, and talked it over and taken their advice on this difficult business.”
“Oh, yes, of course, the Mole and the Badger,” said Toad, airily. “Whatever became of them, the dear fellows? I’d quite forgotten about them.”

“You may well ask!” said the Rat, with a note of reproach. “While you were tearing around the countryside in your pricey motor-cars, galloping proudly on thoroughbreds and dining on the best the land could offer, those two faithful, devoted creatures were camping out in the open in every kind of weather. They lived roughly all day and slept hard all night. They kept watch over your house, patrolled your grounds, never took their eyes off the stoats and weasels, and thought and planned and schemed about how to win your property back for you. Honestly, Toad, you don’t deserve friends so true and loyal. One of these days, when it’s too late, you’ll be sorry you didn’t appreciate them more while you had them!”

“I’m an ungrateful beast, I know,” sobbed Toad, weeping bitter tears. “Let me go out and look for them, out into the cold, dark night, to share their hardships and try to prove by——Wait a moment! Surely that was the clink of dishes on a tray! Supper’s finally here, hooray! Come on, Ratty!”

The Rat bore in mind that poor Toad had lived on prison food for a good long while, and that plenty of allowances had to be made. So he followed Toad to the table and kindly cheered on his brave attempts to make up for everything he’d missed.
They had only just finished eating and settled back into their armchairs when a loud, heavy knocking came at the door.
Toad was nervous, but the Rat gave him a mysterious nod, walked straight up to the door and opened it, and in came Mr. Badger.

He looked like someone who had been kept away from home and all its little comforts for several nights. His shoes were caked with mud, and he was rough and rumpled; but then, he had never been a very smart fellow, the Badger, even at his best. He walked solemnly up to Toad, shook him by the paw, and said, “Welcome home, Toad! Alas! What am I saying? Home, indeed! This is a sorry homecoming. Unhappy Toad!” Then he turned his back on him, sat down at the table, pulled his chair in, and helped himself to a big slice of cold pie.

Toad was quite alarmed by such a grave and ominous greeting; but the Rat whispered to him, “Never mind; take no notice, and don’t say anything to him just yet. He’s always rather gloomy and low when he’s waiting for his food. In half an hour he’ll be a completely different animal.”

So they waited in silence, and soon there came another, lighter knock. The Rat nodded to Toad, went to the door, and showed in the Mole, who looked very shabby and unwashed, with bits of hay and straw stuck in his fur.

“Hooray! Here’s old Toad!” cried the Mole, beaming all over. “Fancy having you back again!” And he began to dance around him. “We never dreamed you’d turn up so soon! Why, you must have escaped, you clever, resourceful, brilliant Toad!”
The Rat, alarmed, tugged at his elbow; but it was too late. Toad was already puffing himself up and swelling.

“Clever? Oh, no!” he said. “According to my friends, I’m not really clever at all. All I’ve done is break out of the toughest prison in England, that’s all! And seize a railway train and get away on it, that’s all! And disguise myself and wander the countryside fooling everybody, that’s all! Oh, no! I’m just a silly fool, I am! Let me tell you about a couple of my little adventures, Mole, and you can decide for yourself!”

“All right, all right,” said Mole, heading for the supper table. “Why don’t you talk while I eat? I haven’t had a bite since breakfast! Oh my! Oh my!” And he took a seat and piled his plate high with cold beef and pickles.

Toad planted his feet wide apart on the hearth-rug, shoved a paw into his trouser pocket, and drew out a fistful of silver coins. “Take a look at that!” he cried, holding it up. “Not bad for a few minutes’ work, eh? And how do you suppose I got it, Mole? Horse-dealing! That’s how I got it!”
“Go on, Toad,” said the Mole, enormously interested.

“Toad, do be quiet, please!” said the Rat. “And don’t you egg him on, Mole, when you know what he’s like. Please just tell us, as soon as you can, how things stand, and what’s best to be done now that Toad is finally back.”

“Things stand about as badly as they possibly could,” replied the Mole grumpily, “and as for what’s to be done, well, I’m blessed if I know! The Badger and I have circled the place again and again, by night and by day, and it’s always the same. Sentries posted everywhere, guns poked out at us, stones thrown at us; always an animal on the lookout, and when they see us, my! how they laugh! That’s what annoys me most!”
“This is a very tricky situation,” said the Rat, deep in thought. “But I believe I can now see, somewhere in the back of my mind, just what Toad ought to do. I’ll tell you. He ought to——”
“No, he oughtn’t!” the Mole shouted through a mouthful of food. “Not at all! You’ve got it wrong. What he ought to do is, he ought to——”

“Well, I won’t do it, whatever you say!” cried Toad, getting worked up. “I refuse to be bossed around by you fellows! We’re talking about my house, and I know exactly what to do, and I’ll tell you. I’m going to——”

Soon all three were talking at once, at the tops of their voices, and the racket was absolutely deafening, when a thin, dry voice cut through it, saying, “Be quiet at once, all of you!” and instantly everyone fell silent.

It was Badger. He had finished his pie, swung around in his chair, and was now giving them a stern look. Once he saw that he had their attention, and that everyone was plainly waiting for him to speak, he turned back to the table and reached for the cheese. Such was the respect that this admirable animal’s sterling qualities commanded that nobody uttered another word until he had completely finished eating and had brushed the crumbs off his knees. Toad squirmed and fidgeted quite a bit, but Rat kept him pinned firmly in his seat.
When the Badger was entirely done, he rose from his seat and stood in front of the fireplace, deep in thought. At last he spoke.

“Toad!” he said sternly. “You wicked, troublesome little creature! Aren’t you ashamed of yourself? What would your father, my dear old friend, have said if he’d been here tonight and known everything you’ve been up to?”
By now Toad was lying on the sofa with his feet up. He rolled over onto his face, shaking with sobs of remorse.

“There, there!” the Badger went on, more kindly. “Never mind. Stop crying. We’re going to let bygones be bygones and make a fresh start. But what the Mole says is quite true. The stoats are on guard at every point, and they make the best sentries in the world. It’s no use at all thinking of attacking the place. They’re too strong for us.”
“Then it’s hopeless,” Toad sobbed into the sofa cushions. “I’ll go and join the army as a soldier, and I’ll never set eyes on my beloved Toad Hall again!”
“Come now, cheer up, Toady!” said Badger. “Storming a place isn’t the only way to win it back. I haven’t had my final say yet. Now I’m going to let you in on a great secret.”

Toad slowly sat up and dried his eyes. Secrets held an enormous attraction for him, because he could never keep one, and he loved the wicked little thrill he felt whenever he went and told another animal, after faithfully promising not to.
“There—is—a—tunnel—underground,” Badger announced solemnly, “which runs from the riverbank, very close to where we sit, all the way to the heart of Toad Hall.”

“Oh, rubbish, Badger!” said Toad, rather breezily. “You’ve been listening to the tall tales people tell in the pubs around here. I know every inch of Toad Hall, inside and out. There’s nothing of the kind, I assure you!”

“Young friend,” said Badger, in a very stern tone, “your father was a decent animal—a good deal more decent than certain others I could name—and a close friend of mine. He told me plenty that he would never have dreamed of telling you. It was he who found that passage. He didn’t build it, of course, since it was dug hundreds of years before he moved in. But he repaired it and cleared it out, thinking it might come in handy someday if there was trouble or danger, and he showed it to me. ‘Don’t let my son hear about it,’ he said. ‘He’s a good lad, but he’s flighty and changeable, and he simply can’t keep a secret. If he ever lands in a truly tight spot where it could help him, then you may tell him about the secret passage—but not a moment sooner.’”
The other animals stared at Toad to see how he would take it. At first Toad was inclined to sulk; but he cheered up at once, like the good fellow he was.

“Well, well,” he said. “Perhaps I do talk rather a lot. When you’re as popular a fellow as I am—my friends crowd around me, we joke, we dazzle, we trade clever stories—and before I know it my tongue has run away with me. I have a gift for conversation, you see. People have told me I ought to run a _salon_, whatever that is. Never mind. Carry on, Badger. How is this tunnel of yours going to help us?”

“I’ve learned a thing or two lately,” Badger went on. “I had Otter dress up as a chimney sweep and turn up at the back door with brushes over his shoulder, asking for work. There’s a big banquet planned for tomorrow night. It’s someone’s birthday—the Chief Weasel’s, I believe—and every weasel will be crowded into the dining-hall, eating and drinking and laughing and making merry, with no suspicion at all. No guns, no swords, no sticks, no weapons of any kind!”
“But the sentries will be posted as usual,” remarked the Rat.

“Precisely,” said Badger. “That’s my point. The weasels will rely completely on their splendid sentries. And that’s where the tunnel comes in. That very handy passage runs straight up beneath the butler’s pantry, right beside the dining-hall!”
“Aha! That squeaky board in the butler’s pantry!” said Toad. “Now I understand!”
“We’ll creep quietly out into the butler’s pantry—” cried the Mole.
“—with our pistols and swords and sticks—” shouted the Rat.
“—and rush in on them,” said the Badger.
“—and thump them, and thump them, and thump them!” shouted Toad in a rapture, dashing around and around the room and leaping over the chairs.

“Very well, then,” said Badger, going back to his usual dry manner. “The plan is decided, so there’s nothing left for you to argue and bicker over. It’s getting very late, so every one of you off to bed this minute. We’ll make all the arrangements we need tomorrow morning.”

Naturally, Toad trooped off to bed along with the others, since he knew better than to refuse, even though he felt far too wound up to sleep. But it had been a long day packed with events, and clean sheets and blankets felt wonderfully welcoming after a thin layer of straw on the stone floor of a drafty cell. Before his head had been on the pillow for more than a few seconds, he was snoring contentedly. He dreamed a great deal, of course. There were roads that ran away from him just when he needed them, and canals that chased him down and caught him, and a barge that sailed into the banqueting-hall carrying his week’s laundry right in the middle of a dinner party he was hosting. Then he was by himself in the secret passage, pushing ahead, but it twisted and turned and gave itself a shake and sat up on end. Even so, in the end he somehow found himself back in Toad Hall, safe and victorious, with all his friends gathered around him, solemnly assuring him that he truly was a clever Toad.

He slept late the next morning, and when he finally came downstairs he found that the other animals had finished breakfast long before. Mole had slipped out alone and hadn’t told a soul where he was off to. Badger was sitting in the armchair with the newspaper, not troubling himself in the least over what would happen that very night. Rat, by contrast, was bustling around the room with his arms full of weapons of every sort, sorting them into four little piles on the floor. As he scurried about he kept muttering excitedly under his breath, “Here’s-a-sword-for-the-Rat, here’s-a-sword-for-the Mole, here’s-a-sword-for-the-Toad, here’s-a-sword-for-the-Badger! Here’s-a-pistol-for-the-Rat, here’s-a-pistol-for-the-Mole, here’s-a-pistol-for-the-Toad, here’s-a-pistol-for-the-Badger!” He went on like that in a steady, singsong way while the four little piles slowly grew taller and taller.

“That’s all well and good, Rat,” Badger said after a while, eyeing the busy little animal over the top of his newspaper. “I’m not criticizing you. But once we’ve gotten past the stoats and those hateful guns of theirs, I promise you we won’t need any swords or pistols. The four of us with our sticks, once we’re inside the dining-hall—well, we’ll sweep every last one of them off the floor in five minutes. I’d have handled the whole thing myself, only I didn’t want to rob you fellows of the fun!”
“It never hurts to play it safe,” said the Rat thoughtfully, rubbing a pistol barrel on his sleeve and peering down the length of it.
When he had finished breakfast, Toad snatched up a sturdy stick and swung it hard, thrashing imaginary animals. “I’ll learn ’em to steal my house!” he cried. “I’ll learn ’em, I’ll learn ’em!”
“Please don’t say ‘learn ’em,’ Toad,” said the Rat, deeply shocked. “That isn’t proper English.”

“Why do you keep nagging at Toad?” asked the Badger, rather irritably. “What’s wrong with his English? It’s just what I speak myself, and if it’s good enough for me, it ought to be good enough for you!”
“Forgive me,” the Rat said humbly. “It’s only that I _believe_ the proper phrase is ‘teach ’em,’ rather than ‘learn ’em.’”
“_Teaching_ ’em is not what we’re after,” snapped the Badger. “We mean to _learn_ ’em—yes, learn ’em, learn ’em! And mark my words, we’ll _manage_ it, too!”

“Oh, all right, whatever you say,” answered the Rat. He had gotten himself rather tangled up over the matter, so he crept off to a corner and mumbled away, “Learn ’em, teach ’em, teach ’em, learn ’em!” over and over, until Badger curtly ordered him to stop.
Soon the Mole came tumbling into the room, obviously very pleased with himself. “I’ve been having such fun!” he began at once. “I’ve been pulling the stoats’ legs!”
“I hope you’ve been very careful, Mole?” said the Rat anxiously.

“I should hope so,” said Mole confidently. “The idea came to me when I went into the kitchen to make sure Toad’s breakfast was being kept warm. There was that old washerwoman outfit he came home in yesterday, hanging over a clothes-horse by the fire. So I put it on, bonnet and shawl and all, and marched off to Toad Hall, bold as brass. The sentries were on watch, naturally, with their guns and their ‘Who goes there?’ and all that other nonsense. ‘Good morning, gentlemen!’ I said, very politely. ‘Any washing you’d like done today?’
“They looked down on me, all proud and stiff and haughty, and said, ‘Be off, washerwoman! We never wash anything while on duty.’ ‘Or at any other time?’ says I. Ho, ho, ho! Wasn’t I _funny_, Toad?”

“Poor, silly creature!” said Toad, in his loftiest manner. The truth was that he was terribly jealous of Mole for what he’d just done. It was precisely what he would have loved to do himself, if only he’d thought of it first and hadn’t gone and slept in.

“Some of the stoats turned quite pink,” the Mole continued, “and the Sergeant in charge said to me, very curtly, he said, ‘Now run away, my good woman, run away! Don’t keep my men idling and chatting at their posts.’ ‘Run away?’ says I. ‘It won’t be me that’s running away, a very short time from now!’”
“Oh, _Moly_, how could you?” said the Rat, dismayed.
The Badger put down his paper.
“I could see them perking up their ears and exchanging looks,” the Mole went on, “and the Sergeant told the others, ‘Pay no attention to _her;_ she hasn’t a notion what she’s talking about.’”

“‘Oh, don’t I?’” said I. “‘Well, let me tell you something. My daughter does the washing for Mr. Badger, so that ought to show you whether I know what I’m talking about. And _you’ll_ find out soon enough, too! A hundred bloodthirsty badgers, armed with rifles, are going to attack Toad Hall tonight, coming in across the paddock. Six boatloads of Rats, with pistols and cutlasses, will row up the river and land in the garden. A hand-picked force of Toads, known as the Die-hards, or the Death-or-Glory Toads, will charge the orchard and sweep everything before them, yelling for revenge. There won’t be much of you left to wash by the time they’re through with you, unless you get out while you still can!’ Then I ran off, and once I was out of sight I hid. After a while I came creeping back along the ditch and peeked at them through the hedge. They were all nervous and flustered, dashing off in every direction at once, tripping over each other, and everybody giving orders to everybody else and nobody listening. The Sergeant kept sending groups of stoats off to far corners of the grounds, and then sending other fellows to fetch them back again. And I heard them grumbling to each other, ‘That’s just like the weasels. They get to stay nice and comfortable in the banqueting hall, with feasting and toasts and songs and all sorts of fun, while we have to stand guard out in the cold and the dark, and in the end get cut to pieces by bloodthirsty Badgers!’”
“Oh, you silly ass, Mole!” cried Toad. “You’ve gone and spoiled everything!”

“Mole,” the Badger said in his quiet, dry manner, “there’s more good sense in your little finger than certain other animals can boast of in their whole plump bodies. You’ve handled everything beautifully, and I’m starting to have great hopes for you. Good Mole! Clever Mole!”

Toad was simply wild with jealousy, especially since he couldn’t for the life of him work out what Mole had done that was so especially clever; but, luckily for him, before he could lose his temper or lay himself open to Badger’s sarcasm, the bell rang for lunch.

The meal was plain but sustaining: bacon, broad beans, and a macaroni pudding. When every plate was clean, the Badger sank into an armchair and announced, “Well, we’ve got our work cut out for us tonight, and it’ll likely be quite late before we’re through, so I’m going to catch forty winks while I can.” Then he drew a handkerchief over his face, and before long he was snoring.

The anxious, hard-working Rat went straight back to his preparations, running to and fro between his four little heaps and muttering, “Here’s-a-belt-for-the-Rat, here’s-a-belt-for-the-Mole, here’s-a-belt-for-the-Toad, here’s-a-belt-for-the-Badger!” and so on, with every new piece of equipment he dug out, of which there seemed to be no end. So Mole slipped his arm through Toad’s, led him out into the fresh air, plopped him into a wicker chair, and made him tell all his adventures from start to finish, which Toad was only too happy to do. Mole was a good listener, and Toad, with nobody to check his claims or criticize him unkindly, let himself go quite freely. In fact, much of what he told belonged more properly to the category of what-might-have-happened-if-I’d-only-thought-of-it-in-time-instead-of ten-minutes-afterwards. Those are always the best and the juiciest adventures; and why shouldn’t they be truly ours, just as much as the rather feeble things that actually happen?
